title: The altar of witness (Joshua 22)
hook: a misunderstood altar nearly starts a war, until people talk

segments.voice: Yesterday, Caleb at eighty-five, asking for the Anakim's hill country. Your line was give me this mountain. Today, an altar by the river, and a near war.

The soldiers are finally going home. For a long time the tribes of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh have fought beside everyone else, though their own land lies east of the Jordan. Joshua blesses them and sends them back across. At the river, they stop and build an altar. A big one, the text says, great to look at. Word reaches the other tribes, and the whole congregation gathers at Shiloh for war. Brothers who just fought side by side are about to fight each other, over a pile of stones nobody has explained.
screen: `THE EASTERN TRIBES GO HOME.` → `A GREAT ALTAR BY THE JORDAN.` → `ISRAEL GATHERS FOR WAR.`

segments.voice: To the other tribes, it looks like betrayal. In the Torah, offerings belong at the one place God chooses, and here is a second altar, on the edge of the land. They remember Peor, where the people strayed, and Achan, whose sin brought trouble on everyone, and they're afraid the whole people will pay again. But before anyone draws a sword, they send people to talk: Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest, with ten princes, one from each tribe. They accuse, and they also offer: if your land feels unclean, come over and take a portion among us. The eastern tribes answer, beginning with God's names, said twice, as if under oath: God knows, and Israel shall know. The altar was never meant for offerings. It was built out of fear. The Jordan runs between us, they say. One day your children might tell our children, you have no portion in the Lord. So we built a copy of the altar, a witness between us, so our children can point at it and say, we belong too. Phinehas hears it, and the mood turns at once: this day we know the Lord is among us. The army goes home. And the eastern tribes name the altar with a reason: "for it shall be a witness between us that the LORD is God." The Hebrew word for witness there is ed, and some translations call the altar Ed. The altar that nearly started a war was built to keep a family together, and nobody knew until somebody asked.
screen: `A SECOND ALTAR LOOKS LIKE BETRAYAL.` · `SEND PEOPLE TO TALK FIRST.` · `WE BUILT IT SO OUR CHILDREN BELONG.` · then, large: `ED: A WITNESS BETWEEN US.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing someone did lately that you've been reading the worst way: a short message, a silence, a change of plans. Notice the story you've already written about it, then write a second one, the way the eastern tribes explained their altar; you don't have to believe it, just hold both. Then shape one question you could ask.
Ed. The altar by the Jordan that looked like rebellion, turned out to be a plea to belong, and was named as a witness. Today's word.
Your line: talk before you fight. The altar was a plea to belong. Day seven hundred eight, in the books.

howItsDone: Jews read Joshua 22 as part of the Former Prophets, and teachers often turn to it as a story about suspicion between communities and the conversation that ended it.

chat.says: Why did the tribes almost go to war over an altar?
options: A second altar looked like rebellion, but it was built as a witness that they belonged.
The eastern tribes really were making offerings there, and backed down when caught.
Phinehas wanted the eastern land, so he used the altar as an excuse to fight.
chat.meaning: They feared their children would be told they had no portion in the Lord, so they built a copy as a witness.

Shiloh.meaning: where the tribes gathered, the sanctuary's place in those days

notes: Auditor: match pair 'the river the eastern tribes feared' (they feared the border, not the river) changed to 'the river they feared would divide them'; KJV source work label made consistent.

Joshua 22:34 is quoted from the KJV; a Keeper may prefer the JPS 1917 wording. The name Ed is supplied by translators (KJV prints it in italics); the Hebrew has only the reason clause, so the script says some translations call the altar Ed.
'Ten princes, one from each tribe' is from Joshua 22:14.
Peor and Achan are both named by the delegation in Joshua 22:17 and 22:20.
The 'one place God chooses' paraphrases Deuteronomy 12; a Keeper may prefer different framing.
God's names said twice paraphrases 22:22 (El Elohim YHWH, repeated); translations differ on rendering it.
